claim: MicrobeFDT is a resource that clusters chemically similar drug and food compounds and links these compounds to microbial enzymes and known toxicities.
source: Here we present MicrobeFDT, a resource which clusters chemically similar drug and food compounds and links these compounds to microbial enzymes and known toxicities.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the resource developed in this study.

claim: Compound structural similarity can serve as a proxy for toxicity.
source: We demonstrate that compound structural similarity can serve as a proxy for toxicity, enzyme sharing, and coarse-grained functional similarity.
evidence: This claim is validated through computational analysis showing correlation between structural and toxicity similarity.

claim: Compound structural similarity can serve as a proxy for enzyme sharing.
source: We demonstrate that compound structural similarity can serve as a proxy for toxicity, enzyme sharing, and coarse-grained functional similarity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of compounds with shared enzymes based on structural similarity.

claim: Compound structural similarity can serve as a proxy for coarse-grained functional similarity.
source: We demonstrate that compound structural similarity can serve as a proxy for toxicity, enzyme sharing, and coarse-grained functional similarity.
evidence: This is validated by showing that structural similarity recapitulates ClassyFire chemical taxonomy.

claim: The gut microbiome metabolizes the ovarian cancer drug altretamine.
source: We validate one such hypothesis experimentally, using MicrobeFDT to reveal unrecognized gut microbiome metabolism of the ovarian cancer drug altretamine.
evidence: This is experimentally validated through LC-MS analysis of fecal slurries showing metabolite formation.

claim: Complex gut microbiome phenotypes shape human nutrition.
source: Complex gut microbiome phenotypes shape human nutrition (Martens et al., 2014; Sonnenburg et al., 2016; Bretin et al., 2018), therapeutic drug responses (Guthrie et al., 2017; Haiser et al., 2013; Koppel et al., 2017) and disease susceptibility (Koeth et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Complex gut microbiome phenotypes shape therapeutic drug responses.
source: Complex gut microbiome phenotypes shape human nutrition (Martens et al., 2014; Sonnenburg et al., 2016; Bretin et al., 2018), therapeutic drug responses (Guthrie et al., 2017; Haiser et al., 2013; Koppel et al., 2017) and disease susceptibility (Koeth et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Complex gut microbiome phenotypes shape disease susceptibility.
source: Complex gut microbiome phenotypes shape human nutrition (Martens et al., 2014; Sonnenburg et al., 2016; Bretin et al., 2018), therapeutic drug responses (Guthrie et al., 2017; Haiser et al., 2013; Koppel et al., 2017) and disease susceptibility (Koeth et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The inactivation and decreased bioavailability of digoxin is linked to cgr operon expression levels in E. lenta.
source: For example, the inactivation and decreased bioavailability of digoxin, a cardiac glycoside inhibitor, is linked to cgr operon expression levels in a single species, E. lenta (Haiser et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Microbial β-glucuronidases mediate the reactivation of the key therapeutic metabolite of irinotecan, causing toxicity in some patients.
source: Microbial β-glucuronidases mediate the reactivation of the key therapeutic metabolite of irinotecan, a chemotherapeutic prodrug used in the treatment of colorectal cancer, causing toxicity in some patients (Guthrie et al., 2017; Wallace et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Diet-derived compounds that are conjugated to glucuronic acid in the human liver and excreted via the biliary route into the GI tract are known substrates for microbial β-glucuronidases.
source: Notably, diet-derived compounds that are conjugated to glucuronic acid in the human liver and excreted via the biliary route into the GI tract are known substrates for microbial β-glucuronidases (O'Leary et al., 2003; Sakurama et al., 2014; Maathuis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Microbial enzymes mediate the conversion of tryptophan into indole.
source: Microbial enzymes mediate the conversion of tryptophan into indole (Sasaki-Imamura et al., 2010) and indole derivatives (Arora and Bae, 2014) that shape human host immune responses (Levy et al., 2017; Blacher et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Microbial enzymes mediate the conversion of tryptophan into indole derivatives that shape human host immune responses.
source: Microbial enzymes mediate the conversion of tryptophan into indole (Sasaki-Imamura et al., 2010) and indole derivatives (Arora and Bae, 2014) that shape human host immune responses (Levy et al., 2017; Blacher et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Microbe produced indole 3-aldehyde functions as an activating ligand for human host aryl hydrocarbon receptors which are expressed by immune cells.
source: Microbe produced indole 3-aldehyde functions as an activating ligand for human host aryl hydrocarbon receptors which are expressed by immune cells (Zelante et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Indole binding induces IL-22 secretion by innate lymphoid cells, promoting the secretion of antimicrobial peptides that protects the host from pathogenic infection by Candida albicans.
source: Indole binding induces IL-22 secretion by innate lymphoid cells, promoting the secretion of antimicrobial peptides that protects the host from pathogenic infection by Candida albicans (Zelante et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Microbial production of short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) from dietary fiber shapes host immunity, contributing to both innate and adaptive immune system functions.
source: Microbial production of short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) from dietary fiber also shapes host immunity, contributing to both innate and adaptive immune system functions (Fukuda et al., 2011; Donohoe et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MicrobeFDT organizes ~10,000 food, drug, and endogenous compounds by structural similarity.
source: We organize ~10,000 food, drug, and endogenous compounds by structural similarity.
evidence: This is a description of the resource developed in the study.

claim: The MicrobeFDT chemical similarity network links 10,822 food, drug, and endogenous compounds with PubChem compound identifier (CIDs).
source: The foundation of the MicrobeFDT resource is a chemical similarity network linking 10,822 food, drug, and endogenous compounds with PubChem compound identifier (CIDs) (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the composition of the network developed in the study.

claim: In the MicrobeFDT network, nodes designate compounds and edges are weighted by pairwise chemical substructure similarity quantified by comparing PubChem fingerprints using the Tanimoto score.
source: In the network, nodes designate compounds and edges are weighted by pairwise chemical substructure similarity quantified by comparing PubChem fingerprints (Kim et al., 2016) using the Tanimoto score (Bajusz et al., 2015) (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the structure of the network and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Compounds with overlapping substructure and physiochemical properties, in which one compound is a known substrate of an enzyme, will be more likely to serve as substrates for the same enzyme.
source: We hypothesized that compounds with overlapping substructure and physiochemical properties, in which one compound is a known substrate of an enzyme, will be more likely to serve as substrates for the same enzyme.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors that is then tested.

claim: The probability estimates of compound-pairs sharing an enzyme based on substructure and physiochemical parameters increase as the substructure overlap score between compound pairs increases.
source: We find that the probability estimates of compound-pairs sharing an enzyme based on substructure and physiochemical parameters, increase as the substructure overlap score between compound pairs increases (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Among the biochemically assayed compounds that are present in the MicrobeFDT network, compounds with substructure similarity scores greater than 0.8 are also substrates for Cgr2.
source: Among the biochemically assayed compounds (Koppel et al., 2018) that are present in the MicrobeFDT network, compounds with substructure similarity scores greater than 0.8 are also substrates for Cgr2.
evidence: This is based on comparison with experimental data from Koppel et al., 2018.

claim: For the cgr enzyme, substructure based clustering can distinguish experimentally characterized substrates from non-substrates.
source: This assessment suggests that for the cgr enzyme substructure based clustering can distinguish experimentally characterized substrates from non-substrates (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Structural similarity moderately positively predicts toxicity similarity for therapeutic drug pairs linked by structural similarity overall in the network (r = 0.03116, p<2.2e-16).
source: We find that structural similarity moderately positively predicts toxicity similarity for therapeutic drug pairs linked by structural similarity overall in the network (r = 0.03116, p<2.2e-16) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Substructure-based compound clustering significantly groups compounds within a ClassyFire superclass based on a comparison of the MicrobeFDT network with a randomized network with the same number of nodes and edges (p<8.06×10–15, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
source: We found that substructure-based compound clustering, significantly groups compounds within a ClassyFire superclass based on a comparison of the MicrobeFDT network with a randomized network with the same number of nodes and edges (p<8.06×10–15, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical comparison with a randomized network.

claim: Compound-pairs at higher substructure similarity share Superclass membership at higher substructure values and at a greater frequency than randomized pairs.
source: Compound-pairs at higher substructure similarity share Superclass membership at higher substructure values and at a greater frequency than randomized pairs, indicating that the MicrobeFDT substructure similarity metric can capture established chemical classifications (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison with randomized networks shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the MicrobeFDT network, therapeutic drug structural diversity is embedded within food-derived chemical diversity.
source: In the network, therapeutic drug structural diversity is embedded within food-derived chemical diversity.
evidence: This is observed from the network structure and composition.

claim: Food derived compounds contributed significantly greater molecular structure diversity than therapeutic drug compounds.
source: Food derived compounds also contributed significantly greater molecular structure diversity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and higher self-similarity than therapeutic drug compounds (two-sample K-S test 0.49, p value=4.7395e-06).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Food derived compounds have higher self-similarity than therapeutic drug compounds (two-sample K-S test 0.49, p value=4.7395e-06).
source: Food derived compounds also contributed significantly greater molecular structure diversity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and higher self-similarity than therapeutic drug compounds (two-sample K-S test 0.49, p value=4.7395e-06).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis.

claim: The ECsD score indicates how broadly distributed a function is across taxa.
source: Thus, the ECsD indicates how broadly distributed a function is, a crucial metric for (1) understanding how to modify a function in the microbiome and (2) predicting how disruptive to the community modifying a function might be.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the ECsD metric developed in the study.

claim: The most commonly synthesized B vitamin across diverse microbial taxa is riboflavin while vitamin B12 is dominated by Fusobacteria.
source: The most commonly synthesized B vitamin across diverse microbial taxa is riboflavin while vitamin B12 is dominated by Fusobacteria (Magnúsdóttir et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The ECsD scores of cobalt-precorrin-2 C(20)-methyltransferase (0.305502) from the anaerobic Vitamin B12 synthesis pathway and riboflavin synthase (0.691618) from the riboflavin synthesis pathway in MicrobeFDT agree with the prior systematic genome assessment and experimental results of Magnúsdóttir et al. (2015).
source: The ECsD scores of cobalt-precorrin-2 C(20)-methyltransferase (0.305502) from the anaerobic Vitamin B12 synthesis pathway and riboflavin synthase (0.691618) from the riboflavin synthesis pathway in MicrobeFDT agree with the prior systematic genome assessment and experimental results of Magnúsdóttir et al. (2015) (Figure 7).
evidence: This validates the ECsD metric against published literature and is shown in Figure 7.

claim: Most bacteria do not synthesize sphingolipids.
source: While most bacteria do not synthesize sphingolipids, sphingolipid biosynthetic capacity has been identified in Sphingomonas spp, Bacteroides and human intestinal pathogens that synthesize and incorporate sphingolipids into their membranes or target host sphingolipids as a point of entry into host cell types (Heaver et al., 2018; Heung et al., 2006; Olsen and Jantzen, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Sphingolipid biosynthetic capacity has been identified in Sphingomonas spp, Bacteroides and human intestinal pathogens.
source: While most bacteria do not synthesize sphingolipids, sphingolipid biosynthetic capacity has been identified in Sphingomonas spp, Bacteroides and human intestinal pathogens that synthesize and incorporate sphingolipids into their membranes or target host sphingolipids as a point of entry into host cell types (Heaver et al., 2018; Heung et al., 2006; Olsen and Jantzen, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The low ECsD score of phosphatidate phosphatase (0.007353), an enzyme involved in sphingolipid biosynthesis and metabolism, mirrors the limited distribution of the sphingolipid biosynthetic capacity across gut microbes.
source: The low ECsD score of phosphatidate phosphatase (0.007353), an enzyme involved in sphingolipid biosynthesis and metabolism (Olsen and Jantzen, 2001), mirrors the limited distribution of the sphingolipid biosynthetic capacity across gut microbes.
evidence: This validates the ECsD metric against known biological information.

claim: Both melamine and altretamine have toxicity profiles that include diarrhea and renal toxicity.
source: Both melamine and altretamine have toxicity profiles that include diarrhea and renal toxicity (Rose et al., 1996; Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Melamine has experimentally validated microbiome-mediated toxicity.
source: Melamine, an industrial compound, has experimentally validated microbiome-mediated toxicity (Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Altretamine toxicity has not previously been linked to an individual's gut microbiota.
source: Altretamine toxicity, however, has not previously been linked to an individual's gut microbiota.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research.

claim: Approximately half of patients taking altretamine orally experience various forms of gastrointestinal toxicity including diarrhea, nausea and/or vomiting.
source: Approximately half of patients taking altretamine orally experience various forms of gastrointestinal toxicity including diarrhea, nausea and/or vomiting (Keldsen et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: N-demethylases in Pseudomonas putida CBB5 enable this microbe to grow on caffeine and other purine alkaloids as the sole carbon and nitrogen source.
source: However, N-demethylases in Pseudomonas putida CBB5 enable this microbe to grow on caffeine and other purine alkaloids as the sole carbon and nitrogen source; thus annotated N-demethylases in P. putida CBB5 can act on compounds that are structurally similar to altretamine (Summers et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Hypothetical proteins homologous to Pseudomonas putida CBB5 N-demethylases are present in a subset of healthy human guts.
source: Furthermore, we identify hypothetical proteins homologous to Pseudomonas putida CBB5 N-demethylases in a subset of healthy human guts (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gut microbial N-demethylases may partially or completely N-demethylate altretamine, converting it into metabolites that contribute to patient toxicity.
source: We hypothesized that gut microbial N-demethylases may partially or completely N-demethylate altretamine, converting it into metabolites that contribute to patient toxicity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on network analysis.

claim: A metabolite that is structurally identical to pentamethylmelamine, a demethylated altretamine metabolite, increases in active fecal microcosms over 48 hr.
source: We controlled for the formation of spontaneous N-demethylation of altretamine, which has been reported in the literature (Damia and D'Incalci, 1995), and found that a metabolite that is structurally identical to pentamethylmelamine, a demethylated altretamine metabolite, increases in active fecal microcosms over 48 hr (Figure 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated through LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: In active fecal biotic conditions the metabolite continually increased between time 0 and 48 hr.
source: In active fecal biotic conditions the metabolite continually increased between time 0 and 48 hr.
evidence: This is observed from the experimental data.

claim: Killed controls demonstrated an increase in metabolite between 0 and 24 hr, though to a lesser extent than in active fecal microcosms.
source: Killed controls demonstrated an increase in metabolite between 0 and 24 hr, though to a lesser extent than in active fecal microcosms.
evidence: This is observed from the experimental data.

claim: There was little metabolite formation after 24 hr in killed controls.
source: Notably there was little metabolite formation after 24 hr, indicating that in addition to abiotic N-demethylation, active gut microbes demethylate altretamine to the putative metabolite pentamethylmelamine.
evidence: This is observed from the experimental data.

claim: In addition to abiotic N-demethylation, active gut microbes demethylate altretamine to the putative metabolite pentamethylmelamine.
source: Notably there was little metabolite formation after 24 hr, indicating that in addition to abiotic N-demethylation, active gut microbes demethylate altretamine to the putative metabolite pentamethylmelamine.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of active and killed controls.

claim: Conjugated primary bile acids function as potent detergents and antimicrobial agents capable of dissolving microbial membranes and causing intracellular acidification.
source: Conjugated primary bile acids (BA) function as potent detergents and antimicrobial agents capable of dissolving microbial membranes and causing intracellular acidification; bile acid function is linked to specific structural features of these compounds (Jones et al., 2008; Begley et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Bile acid function is linked to specific structural features of these compounds.
source: Conjugated primary bile acids (BA) function as potent detergents and antimicrobial agents capable of dissolving microbial membranes and causing intracellular acidification; bile acid function is linked to specific structural features of these compounds (Jones et al., 2008; Begley et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA) is a taurine conjugated primary bile acid with a diet-tunable concentration in the gut.
source: Taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA) is a taurine conjugated primary bile acid with a diet-tunable concentration in the gut (Ridlon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Energy drinks, animal protein and fish are rich sources of taurine while vegetarian and vegan diets dominated by fruits, vegetables, legumes and soy are poor sources.
source: Energy drinks, animal protein and fish are rich sources of taurine while vegetarian and vegan diets dominated by fruits, vegetables, legumes and soy are poor sources (Ridlon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Taurine conjugated bile acids are hypothesized to contribute to the etiology of colorectal cancer by generating hydrogen sulfide during microbial mediated de-conjugation of taurine conjugates.
source: Taurine conjugated bile acids are hypothesized to contribute to the etiology of colorectal cancer by generating hydrogen sulfide during microbial mediated de-conjugation of taurine conjugates (Ridlon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Glycocholic and taurocholic conjugated bile acids are bacteriostatic, inhibiting S. aureus growth by decreasing intracellular pH and disrupting the proton motor force.
source: Conjugated primary bile acids have demonstrated in vitro activity as antimicrobial compounds, for example glycocholic and taurocholic conjugated bile acids are bacteriostatic, inhibiting S. aureus growth by decreasing intracellular pH and disrupting the proton motor force (Sannasiddappa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Bile salt hydrolase (BSH) mediated bile salt deconjugation is one mechanism that gut microbes use to detoxify conjugated primary bile acids.
source: Bile salt hydrolase (BSH) mediated bile salt deconjugation is one mechanism that gut microbes use to detoxify conjugated primary bile acids (Begley et al., 2006); thus BSH activity may support gut bacterial persistence in face of frequent contact with primary BAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: BSH activity may support gut bacterial persistence in face of frequent contact with primary BAs.
source: Bile salt hydrolase (BSH) mediated bile salt deconjugation is one mechanism that gut microbes use to detoxify conjugated primary bile acids (Begley et al., 2006); thus BSH activity may support gut bacterial persistence in face of frequent contact with primary BAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the detoxification function of BSH.

claim: BSH enzymes are phylogenetically diverse and abundant across healthy human fecal metagenomes.
source: BSH enzymes are phylogenetically diverse and abundant across healthy human fecal metagenomes (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: In a Wistar rat model of chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP), finasteride reduces bacterial infection as a single agent and has a synergistic effect with ciprofloxacin through an unknown mechanism.
source: Notably, in a Wistar rat model of chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP), finasteride reduces bacterial infection as a single agent and has a synergistic effect with ciprofloxacin through an unknown mechanism (Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Chavex-Dozal and colleagues propose a role for finasteride in the prevention of Candida albicans biofilm formation and filamentation through in vitro studies.
source: Through in vitro studies, Chavex-Dozal and colleagues propose a role for finasteride in the prevention of Candida albicans biofilm formation and filamentation (Chavez-Dozal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Finasteride may have unrecognized off-target antibiotic effects.
source: These experimental results support the hypothesis that finasteride may have unrecognized off-target antibiotic effects.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on cited literature.

claim: Dexamethasone has dose-dependent anti-microbial activity against clinically isolated Streptococcus milleri, Aspergillus flavus, and Aspergillus fumigatus in culture, while not killing Staphylococcus aureus.
source: Dexamethasone has known anti-microbial properties. For example, dexamethasone has dose-dependent anti-microbial activity against clinically isolated Streptococcus milleri, Aspergillus flavus, and Aspergillus fumigatus in culture, while not killing Staphylococcus aureus (Neher et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa was found to be susceptible to dexamethasone at high concentrations.
source: Pseudomonas aeruginosa was found to be susceptible to dexamethasone at high concentrations (Neher et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Cortisone has been linked to a variety of opportunistic infections by enteric bacterial pathogens, for example an increase in gastrointestinal parasites and reactivation of Chlamydia pneumoniae.
source: Cortisone, which also has significant structural overlap with TCDCA, has been linked to a variety of opportunistic infections by enteric bacterial pathogens, for example an increase in gastrointestinal parasites (Nair et al., 1981) and reactivation of Chlamydia pneumoniae (Laitinen et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Steviol is a component of stevia which has antimicrobial properties against Borrelia burgdorferi in vitro.
source: Steviol is a component of stevia which has antimicrobial properties against Borrelia burgdorferi in vitro (Theophilus et al., 2015), and lanosterol derivatives have antifungal activities (Shingate, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Lanosterol derivatives have antifungal activities.
source: Steviol is a component of stevia which has antimicrobial properties against Borrelia burgdorferi in vitro (Theophilus et al., 2015), and lanosterol derivatives have antifungal activities (Shingate, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Tomatidine was recently identified as an antibiotic molecule that inhibits ATP synthesis against Staphylococcus aureus.
source: Tomatidine was recently identified as an antibiotic molecule that inhibits ATP synthesis against Staphylococcus aureus (Lamontagne Boulet et al., 2018); we hypothesize that the antimicrobial activity of this compound may include intracellular acidification given its structural overlap with TCDCA (Figure 10d).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The antimicrobial activity of tomatidine may include intracellular acidification given its structural overlap with TCDCA.
source: Tomatidine was recently identified as an antibiotic molecule that inhibits ATP synthesis against Staphylococcus aureus (Lamontagne Boulet et al., 2018); we hypothesize that the antimicrobial activity of this compound may include intracellular acidification given its structural overlap with TCDCA (Figure 10d).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on structural similarity.

claim: In addition to modulating immune responses, bile salt-like compounds may selectively alter human microbiomes.
source: We propose that in addition to modulating immune responses, bile salt-like compounds may selectively alter human microbiomes, again, with unknown consequences for treatment outcomes and health.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: β-glucuronidases play a major role in the toxicity of the colorectal cancer chemotherapeutic prodrug irinotecan (CPT-11).
source: β-glucuronidases play a major role in the toxicity of the colorectal cancer chemotherapeutic prodrug irinotecan (CPT-11), whose active form, SN-38, is inactivated by hepatic glucuronidation and excreted into the gut as the inactive metabolite SN-38 glucuronide (SN-38G) (Wallace et al., 2010; Sparreboom et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The active form of irinotecan, SN-38, is inactivated by hepatic glucuronidation and excreted into the gut as the inactive metabolite SN-38 glucuronide (SN-38G).
source: β-glucuronidases play a major role in the toxicity of the colorectal cancer chemotherapeutic prodrug irinotecan (CPT-11), whose active form, SN-38, is inactivated by hepatic glucuronidation and excreted into the gut as the inactive metabolite SN-38 glucuronide (SN-38G) (Wallace et al., 2010; Sparreboom et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Microbial β-glucuronidases hydrolyze the glucuronide group, releasing the aglycone SN-38 into the intestinal environment.
source: Microbial β-glucuronidases hydrolyze the glucuronide group, releasing the aglycone SN-38 into the intestinal environment (Figure 11a).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 11a.

claim: Deconjugation of SN-38G promotes epithelial damage and severe diarrhea in some patients and in mouse models.
source: Deconjugation promotes epithelial damage and severe diarrhea in some patients and in mouse models (Wallace et al., 2010; Sparreboom et al., 1998; Slatter et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Individual human fecal samples have variable capacities to deconjugate SN-38G.
source: We previously demonstrated that individual human fecal samples have variable capacities to deconjugate SN-38G (Guthrie et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Most compounds identified as significantly similar to SN-38G were food derivatives or other constituents.
source: Most compounds identified as significantly similar to SN-38G were food derivatives or other constituents (Figure 11b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11b.

claim: Flavonoids such as baicalin and scutellarin are widely distributed in plants.
source: Among these targets were flavonoids such as baicalin and scutellarin which are widely distributed in plants (Kumar and Pandey, 2013) (Figure 11c).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Flavonoids such as baicalin and scutellarin may compete with SN-38G for turnover by microbial β-glucuronidases and are a potential avenue for decreasing the adverse drug responses associated with irinotecan administration.
source: We propose that these compounds may compete with SN-38G for turnover by microbial β-glucuronidases and are a potential avenue for decreasing the adverse drug responses associated with irinotecan administration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on network analysis.

claim: The MicrobeFDT database encompasses 13,440 nodes including 10,822 xenobiotic, diet-derived and human gut endogenous compounds, 2062 microbial enzymes and 525 therapeutic drug use labels.
source: The MicrobeFDT graph database encodes heterogeneous information on the interactions between compounds and microbial enzymes in the gut chemical landscape, highlighting the following four relationships across 13,440 nodes (10,822 xenobiotic, diet-derived and human gut endogenous compounds, 2062 microbial enzymes and 525 therapeutic drug use labels) defined from publicly available data directly or computed: (1) compound-compound substructure similarity; (2) compound-compound toxicity similarity; (3) microbial enzyme-compound interactions; and (4) drug-indication associations.
evidence: This describes the composition of the MicrobeFDT database.

claim: The MicrobeFDT database defines four types of relationships: compound-compound substructure similarity, compound-compound toxicity similarity, microbial enzyme-compound interactions, and drug-indication associations.
source: The MicrobeFDT graph database encodes heterogeneous information on the interactions between compounds and microbial enzymes in the gut chemical landscape, highlighting the following four relationships across 13,440 nodes (10,822 xenobiotic, diet-derived and human gut endogenous compounds, 2062 microbial enzymes and 525 therapeutic drug use labels) defined from publicly available data directly or computed: (1) compound-compound substructure similarity; (2) compound-compound toxicity similarity; (3) microbial enzyme-compound interactions; and (4) drug-indication associations.
evidence: This describes the types of relationships in the MicrobeFDT database.

claim: The MicrobeFDT database is implemented in Neo4j and can be queried through the Cypher Query Language.
source: The database is implemented in Neo4j (https://neo4j.com/) and can be queried through the Cypher Query Language.
evidence: This describes the technical implementation of the database.

claim: The formation of metabolite 1 at 24 and 48 hr was significantly increased under the experimental condition in comparison to the contribution of spontaneous N-demethylation by an unpaired two-sample Wilcoxon test (*=P < 0.05).
source: The formation of metabolite 1 at 24 and 48 hr was significantly increased under the experimental condition in comparison to the contribution of spontaneous N-demethylation by an unpaired two-sample Wilcoxon test (*=P < 0.05).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 9.
